title: PlayerOne: Egocentric World Simulator

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The rotation matrix formula is written R = I + sinθ·[u]_× + (1 + cosθ)·[u]_×², but the standard Rodrigues' formula is R = I + sinθ·[u]_× + (1 − cosθ)·[u]_×². With the published sign, θ = π about z gives R = I instead of the expected 2uuᵀ − I, and θ = π/2 maps (1,0,0) to (−1,1,0) instead of (0,1,0).

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract vs Section 4.1 (Implementation details) vs Appendix (Latency)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Abstract claims 'true real-time generation at 30 FPS', while Section 4.1 states 'After distillation, our method can achieve 8 FPS' and the appendix reports ~119 ms/frame ≈ 8.4 FPS. The 30 FPS figure is a ~3.5× overstatement inconsistent with both the methods section and the appendix.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix Table 8 (Comparison with works in autonomous driving)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 8 labels rows 'GEM [8]' and 'VISTA [15]', but reference [8] is VISTA (Gao et al.) and reference [15] is GEM (Hassan et al.). The citation numbers are swapped.

References [24] and [25] both point to the same paper (Nymeria: A Massive Collection of Multimodal Egocentric Daily Motion in the Wild, ECCV 2024) with overlapping author lists. The same work is cited under two different numbers (used as [24] in Table 1 and as [25] in Sections 4.1/4.2), a duplicate reference entry.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 (Benchmark) vs Appendix A (Evaluation on Nymeria)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 states the benchmark is '100 videos collected from the Nymeria [25] dataset, which is not included for training', but Appendix A states 'we selected 100 videos featuring full-body actions from the test sets of four different datasets: EgoExo-4D, Nymeria, FT-HID, EgoExo-Fitness'. Two irreconcilable descriptions of the same 100-video benchmark.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2 (Scene-frame reconstruction) vs Appendix (Details of training pipeline)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main text says 'point maps are only required during the training phase. During inference, the system simplifies the process by utilizing only the first frame and the corresponding human motion sequence', while the appendix asserts 'the scene-consistency module remains fully active during inference... Inference keeps the joint two-stream denoising (video + point maps)'. The two descriptions of the inference design directly contradict each other.

Rows in Tables 18 and 19 that represent the same final model share DINO 67.8 / CLIP 88.2 with Tables 2 and 3 but report different MRRPE (163.62 vs 151.62), PSNR (50.3 vs 52.6), and FVD (236.12 vs 226.12). No benchmark difference is stated to explain the mismatch, and these values also differ from the Nymeria-benchmark numbers in Tables 5/6.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix (Investigation on the impact of filtering) / Table 19
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'a filtering ratio of 10% optimizes performance' and 'the absence of filtering also causes performance deterioration', but Table 19 shows that at 0% filtering MPJPE (123.50), MRRPE (158.10), PSNR (47.5), FVD (228.50), and LPIPS (0.0587) are all BETTER than at 10% (127.16 / 163.62 / 50.3 / 236.12 / 0.0663). Only DINO/CLIP peak at 10%, so the table contradicts the claim.

'Qwen2.5-VL [2]' is cited to reference [2], which is the original 'Qwen Technical Report' (arXiv:2309.16609, Sept 2023) describing the base Qwen/Qwen1.5 models. This predates Qwen2.5-VL and cannot be the source for the Qwen2.5-VL captioning claim; the Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report (arXiv:2502.13923) is the appropriate reference.

Table 2's final row 'PlayerOne (ours, indoor scenes only)' carries exactly the same seven numbers as Table 3's unqualified 'PlayerOne (ours)' row and the appendix's 'Real' domain row in Table 14, which is inconsistent with the claimed full-benchmark evaluation over diverse indoor/outdoor/game scenarios.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.3 (User study) vs Appendix (Definition of evaluation criteria)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Main text says 'We let 20 annotators rate 25 groups of videos' against 'the text description', while the appendix says annotators rated 'all 100 videos' side-by-side against the 'motion condition signal (stick-figure or pose sequence)'. Both the sample size and the reference condition differ between the two accounts (25 groups × 4 methods could reconcile counts, but this is never stated).

The Introduction says the human motion sequence 'is partitioned into three groups (i.e., head, hands, feet and body)', enumerating four items under 'three groups', whereas Section 3.2 correctly gives three groups (body and feet, hands, head). A self-contradictory enumeration.

Both tables report the 'PlayerOne (ours)' row on the same Nymeria benchmark: DINO 64.87 vs 64.80 and CLIP 85.79 vs 85.70 differ while all five other metrics agree to multiple decimals, indicating a transcription error.
'we utilize 49 video frames (6 seconds) for training' — 49 frames at 8 FPS is 6.125 s, not 6 s. A minor rounding discrepancy between the stated exact figures.

summary: Uncertainty-mode verification of 'PlayerOne: Egocentric World Simulator' (cs.CV) with lenient strictness routed 28 high-uncertainty snippets to specialist verifiers (math, statistical, text, citation, cross-section). 14 findings survived, including several high-confidence errors: (1) Equation 3 uses the wrong sign in Rodrigues' rotation formula (1+cosθ instead of 1−cosθ), which invalidates the stated rotation matrix (0.97); (2) the abstract claims 30 FPS real-time generation while the methods section and appendix report 8 FPS / 8.4 FPS (0.95); (3) Table 8 swaps the GEM and VISTA citation numbers (0.95); (4) reference [24] and [25] are duplicate entries for the same Nymeria paper (0.90); (5) the benchmark is described as Nymeria-only in the main text but as spanning four datasets in the appendix (0.85); and (6) the main text says point maps are not used at inference while the appendix states the point-map stream remains fully active at inference (0.85). Additional medium-confidence issues include numeric mismatches between Tables 18/19 and Tables 2/3 for the same model row, a filtering-ratio claim contradicted by Table 19, a Qwen2.5-VL mis-citation, an 'indoor scenes only' row label carrying full-model numbers, and user-study/benchmark count discrepancies. Because multiple findings exceed 0.85 confidence, the paper requires correction.
